title: Heartburn After Drinking: Why It Happens, Worst Drinks & Antacids
excerpt: Why alcohol causes heartburn, which drinks are the worst offenders, how to time Tums and Pepcid so they actually help, and the warning signs that mean it isn't heartburn.
metaDescription: Why alcohol causes heartburn, which drinks are worst, how to time Tums and Pepcid, how to prevent it, and when chest pain after drinking needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** heartburn after drinking is very common, and for most people it's a short-lived nuisance rather than a sign of something serious. Alcohol loosens the muscle that normally keeps stomach acid out of your food pipe, some drinks push your stomach to make more acid, and the things that tend to go with a night out (fizzy mixers, big late meals, lying down soon after) make all of it worse. The good news is that most of it is predictable, which means most of it is preventable. This guide explains why it happens, which drinks are the worst offenders, how to time antacids so they actually help, and the warning signs that mean it isn't heartburn at all.

**The quick rules:** Choose still drinks over fizzy ones, and drier wine or spirits with a non-carbonated mixer over beer, sweet cocktails, and champagne. Eat a moderate meal early rather than a heavy meal late. Stop drinking and eating two to three hours before bed, and sleep on your left side with your head raised if you're prone to reflux. A chewable antacid works within minutes but wears off fast. A preventive acid reducer like famotidine needs to be taken before you start, not after the burning begins. Avoid aspirin-based fizzy remedies after drinking.

> **When to see a doctor (and when to call 911).** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** chest pain spreads to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or lightheadedness, or feels like pressure or squeezing rather than burning. Heart attacks can feel like heartburn, and you should never assume. **Also get emergency care if** you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, or have severe stomach pain that won't settle. **See a doctor soon if** you get heartburn more than twice a week, it wakes you at night, over-the-counter remedies have stopped working, food feels like it sticks when you swallow, you're losing weight without trying, or you have a lasting hoarse voice or cough. If you're shaking, sweating, or feeling anxious and unwell the morning after very heavy drinking, especially after several days in a row, that can be alcohol withdrawal and needs medical attention rather than an antacid.

## What Heartburn Actually Is

Heartburn has nothing to do with your heart. It's a burning feeling behind the breastbone, sometimes rising into the throat, caused by stomach acid flowing back up into the esophagus (the tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach). Doctors call this backflow **acid reflux**. When it happens often and causes symptoms or damage, it's called **gastroesophageal reflux disease**, or GERD.

Your stomach is built to handle strong acid. Its lining has a thick protective mucus layer. Your esophagus has no such protection, so when acid gets in, it burns.

What normally keeps the acid where it belongs is a ring of muscle at the bottom of the esophagus called the **lower esophageal sphincter** (LES). Think of it as a one-way valve. It opens to let food down, then closes tight. Heartburn happens when that valve relaxes when it shouldn't, or when pressure in the stomach pushes acid past it.

You might also notice a sour or bitter taste in your mouth, burping, a feeling that food is coming back up (regurgitation), or a dry cough or hoarse voice the next morning. Those are all part of the same reflux picture.

## Why Alcohol Gives You Heartburn

Alcohol pushes on the problem from several directions at once. That's why even people who rarely get heartburn can feel it after a big night.

### 1. It relaxes the valve

Alcohol lowers the pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter. Studies measuring that pressure directly have shown it drops after drinking, which makes it easier for acid to slip upward. This effect is the main reason heartburn tracks so closely with drinking.

### 2. It slows the clean-up

Your esophagus normally clears any acid that does reflux by squeezing it back down with waves of muscle movement, and by washing it with swallowed saliva, which is slightly alkaline. Research on esophageal motility suggests alcohol can weaken those clearing waves. So acid that gets up there tends to stay longer, which is when it does the most burning.

### 3. Some drinks boost acid production

This is the part most people don't know. Not all alcoholic drinks act on the stomach in the same way. Research in gastroenterology going back decades found that **fermented drinks like beer and wine strongly stimulate stomach acid**, while pure ethanol and distilled spirits such as whisky have much weaker effects on acid output. The trigger appears to be other compounds produced during fermentation, not the alcohol itself. So a pint of beer may push acid production up more than a shot of whiskey with the same amount of alcohol.

That doesn't make spirits "safe." They still relax the valve and irritate the lining, and stronger drinks can irritate the esophagus directly on the way down. But it helps explain why some people find beer and wine much worse than a simple spirit drink.

### 4. It irritates the stomach and esophagus lining

High concentrations of alcohol can irritate and inflame the lining of the stomach (gastritis) and esophagus. An irritated lining is more sensitive to acid, so the same amount of reflux hurts more. This is also why heartburn after drinking often comes with general stomach upset. If your main problem is a sore or aching stomach rather than a burning chest, our guide to [hangover nausea and stomach relief](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers that side.

### 5. The night-out extras

Drinking rarely happens on its own. Several things that travel with it are classic reflux triggers:

- **Carbonation.** Bubbles expand the stomach, which raises pressure and triggers the valve to open briefly so you can burp. Acid can escape along with the gas.
- **Big, late, fatty meals.** A full stomach presses harder on the valve, and fatty food slows stomach emptying, so there's more in there for longer. Pizza, burgers, fries, and kebabs at midnight are a reflux setup.
- **Spicy food, citrus, tomato, chocolate, and mint.** These are common personal triggers for many people with reflux.
- **Lying down soon after.** Gravity is one of your best defenses. When you lie flat, acid can flow up much more easily.
- **Smoking or vaping.** Nicotine also relaxes the valve, and many people smoke more when they drink.
- **Caffeine.** Coffee-based cocktails, energy drink mixers, and cola all add caffeine, which bothers some people's reflux.

Put it together and a typical night out (several beers or fizzy cocktails, a heavy late meal, straight into bed) stacks nearly every reflux risk on top of each other.

## Which Drinks Cause the Most Heartburn?

There's no official ranking, and everyone's triggers differ. But based on the mechanisms above, here's a reasonable guide to which drinks are more and less likely to cause trouble.

| Drink | Heartburn risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Champagne, prosecco, sparkling wine | Higher | Carbonation plus fermentation plus acidity |
| Beer, especially in large volumes | Higher | Carbonation, fermentation compounds, and volume all fill and stretch the stomach |
| Hard seltzer and spiked sparkling drinks | Moderate to higher | Carbonation and often citric acid |
| Cocktails with soda, cola, tonic, or energy drinks | Higher | Carbonation, sugar, acidity, and sometimes caffeine |
| Citrus-heavy cocktails (margaritas, sours) | Moderate to higher | Acidic mixers irritate an already sensitive esophagus |
| Red and white wine | Moderate | Fermentation stimulates acid; wine is also acidic. Many people with reflux report white wine bothers them more, but this varies |
| Coffee liqueurs and espresso martinis | Moderate to higher | Alcohol plus caffeine |
| Spirits neat or with still water | Lower to moderate | Weaker effect on acid production, no bubbles, but high strength can irritate |
| Spirits with a non-citrus, non-fizzy mixer | Lower to moderate | Lower volume, no carbonation |

The general pattern is that **volume, bubbles, and acidity are your enemies**. If you're prone to heartburn, a single spirit with still water will usually bother you less than three pints of beer or a bottle of sparkling wine, even if the amount of alcohol is similar.

The biggest factor is still how much you drink. Population research, including meta-analyses pooling many studies, has linked heavier drinking with a higher risk of reflux disease, and the risk appears to rise with the amount consumed. Switching drinks helps, but drinking less helps most.

## Heartburn the Morning After

Many people notice heartburn isn't just a during-the-night problem. It can show up or linger the next morning. A few reasons:

- **Your stomach lining is still irritated.** It takes time for alcohol-related irritation to calm down.
- **You slept flat with a full stomach.** Hours of nighttime reflux can leave your esophagus sore, and a raw esophagus burns more easily when you eat or drink anything acidic in the morning.
- **Coffee and greasy breakfasts.** The classic hangover breakfast of strong coffee, orange juice, and a fried plate adds more triggers to an already irritated system.
- **Painkillers.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate the stomach lining themselves, and alcohol makes that worse. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the stomach bleeding warning in detail. If you have heartburn the morning after and need pain relief, ask a pharmacist which option suits you.
- **Vomiting.** If you were sick during the night, stomach acid has already passed through your esophagus and throat, leaving them inflamed.

For a morning-after flare, think gentle: water, a bland breakfast like toast, oatmeal, or bananas, and skip the coffee or orange juice until things settle. Sit upright for a while after eating.

## Antacid Timing: How to Get the Most From Each Type

The three main types of heartburn medicine work very differently, and timing is where most people go wrong. These are general points from the products' labels and standard pharmacology. Always follow your specific product's label and ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

| Type | Examples | How it works | Speed | How long it lasts | Best timing for drinking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Antacids | Tums, Rolaids, Gaviscon, Mylanta | Neutralize acid already in the stomach | Within minutes | Short, often under an hour or two | When symptoms start, or soon after a meal |
| H2 blockers | Famotidine (Pepcid AC) | Reduce how much acid the stomach makes | Usually within an hour | Several hours, often up to around 12 | Before you start, following the label's prevention directions |
| Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) | Omeprazole (Prilosec OTC), esomeprazole (Nexium 24HR), lansoprazole | Strongly shut down acid production | Slow, can take a few days for full effect | Around 24 hours per dose | Not designed for a one-off night out |

### Antacids (Tums, Rolaids, Gaviscon)

These are quick, cheap, and good for occasional heartburn. They don't stop acid being made. They simply neutralize what's there, so the relief is fast but short. If you take one at 10 p.m. and keep drinking until 1 a.m., it will likely have worn off long before you go to bed.

Some products, such as Gaviscon, also contain alginate, which forms a foam layer on top of the stomach contents that helps keep acid from rising. Many people find these useful at bedtime.

Tips:

- **Take them when symptoms appear, or after eating**, and stay within the label's daily maximum. Calcium-based antacids like [Tums](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) have a daily limit for a reason, since too much calcium can cause problems.
- **Check for interactions.** Antacids can affect how well some other medicines are absorbed, including certain antibiotics and thyroid medicine. Spacing doses apart is often enough, but ask a pharmacist.
- **They aren't a license to keep drinking.** Masking the burn doesn't change what alcohol is doing to the valve and lining.

### H2 blockers (famotidine)

Famotidine reduces how much acid your stomach makes, and it lasts much longer than an antacid. The US label for Pepcid AC includes directions for preventing heartburn by taking it shortly before eating food or drinking beverages that cause symptoms (the label gives a window of roughly 15 to 60 minutes). That makes it the most useful option if you already know a particular dinner and drinks will set you off.

On alcohol itself: famotidine is not known to have a significant interaction with alcohol for most people. Some older acid reducers in this class were studied for slightly raising blood alcohol levels, but famotidine has shown little or no such effect in research. That said, reducing your heartburn doesn't reduce any other harm from drinking. Stick to the label dose, and if you need famotidine regularly, that's a reason to see a doctor rather than a reason to keep self-treating.

### Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole and similar)

PPIs are the most powerful acid reducers, but they're built for frequent heartburn, not for one night. They work best when taken daily before breakfast and can take a few days to reach full effect. The over-the-counter labels describe a 14-day course for frequent heartburn. If you find yourself wanting a PPI regularly because of drinking, that pattern is worth discussing with a doctor.

### Remedies to be careful with after drinking

- **Alka-Seltzer Original** and similar fizzy tablets contain aspirin along with the antacid. Aspirin plus alcohol raises the risk of stomach bleeding. There are aspirin-free versions, so read the label carefully.
- **Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol)** contains a salicylate, a relative of aspirin. It can be useful for an upset stomach, but people who are allergic to aspirin, take blood thinners, or are on certain other medicines should check first. It can also temporarily turn your tongue or stools black, which is harmless but can be confused with bleeding.
- **Baking soda in water** is an old home remedy that does neutralize acid, but it's high in sodium and isn't a good idea for people with high blood pressure, heart, or kidney problems. It also releases gas in the stomach.

## How to Prevent Heartburn When You Drink

You'll get more out of a few habits than out of any pill.

### Before you drink

- **Eat a moderate meal, early.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, which is good. But an enormous meal right before or during drinking adds pressure on the valve. Aim for a normal-sized meal a few hours before bed.
- **Know your triggers.** If spicy food, tomato sauce, or chocolate set you off, a night of drinking isn't the time to add them.
- **If you're prone to heartburn**, consider taking a preventive acid reducer according to its label before you start, rather than reacting later.

### While you drink

- **Pick still over sparkling.** Swap beer or champagne for a spirit with still water, or wine without bubbles.
- **Avoid fizzy and acidic mixers.** Soda, cola, tonic, energy drinks, and heavy citrus all add triggers.
- **Alternate with water.** It dilutes alcohol in the stomach and slows your pace. Plain water, not sparkling.
- **Slow down and drink less.** Fewer drinks means less valve relaxation and less irritation. This is the most effective single change.
- **Skip the cigarettes and vapes.** Nicotine relaxes the valve too.

### After you drink

- **Stop eating and drinking two to three hours before bed** if you can. This gives your stomach time to empty.
- **Avoid the late-night greasy food run.** If you must eat, keep it small and plain.
- **Raise the head of your bed.** Lifting your upper body by around 15 to 20 cm, with blocks under the bed legs or a wedge pillow, works better than stacking regular pillows, which can bend you at the waist and squeeze your stomach.
- **Sleep on your left side.** Research on nighttime reflux suggests left-side sleeping leads to less reflux than right-side sleeping, likely because of how the stomach sits relative to the esophagus.
- **Loosen tight waistbands.** Pressure on your belly pushes on your stomach.

More broadly, the habits that help with heartburn overlap heavily with the ones that make for a better morning. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing, food, and hydration in more depth.

## Natural Remedies: What Has Evidence and What Doesn't

You'll see lots of home remedies for heartburn online. Here's an honest look at the common ones.

- **Water.** A few sips can help wash acid back down. Simple and harmless.
- **Chewing gum.** Chewing increases saliva, which is slightly alkaline and helps clear the esophagus. Some small studies support this after meals. Avoid mint flavors, which may relax the valve.
- **Milk.** It may feel soothing for a moment, but the fat and protein can stimulate more acid afterward. There is no good evidence that it helps heartburn overall.
- **Apple cider vinegar.** Popular online, but there is no good evidence that it helps heartburn, and it's acidic, so it may make an irritated esophagus worse.
- **Ginger.** Has some evidence for nausea, and some people find it settles their stomach. There is no good evidence that it treats reflux specifically, and large amounts can cause heartburn in some people.
- **Bananas, oatmeal, and plain toast.** Bland, low-acid foods are a sensible choice for a sore stomach the morning after, even if they don't treat reflux directly.

## Is It Heartburn, or Something Else?

Chest discomfort after drinking isn't always reflux. It's worth knowing the difference.

- **Heart attack or heart rhythm problems.** As mentioned at the top, a heart attack can feel like heartburn, particularly in women, older adults, and people with diabetes. Heavy drinking can also trigger an irregular heartbeat in some people (sometimes called "holiday heart"), which can feel like fluttering, racing, or pounding, along with breathlessness or dizziness. If you're not sure, get checked. It's far better to be told it was reflux than to wait at home with a heart problem.
- **Gastritis or an ulcer.** Burning or gnawing pain in the upper stomach, often with nausea, can point to stomach lining inflammation or an ulcer, especially if you also take NSAID painkillers. Black stools or vomiting blood are emergencies.
- **Pancreatitis.** Severe, steady pain in the upper belly that may spread to your back, often with vomiting, can follow heavy drinking. This is a medical emergency.
- **Gallbladder problems.** Pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal can come from the gallbladder rather than reflux.
- **Esophageal tear.** Forceful, repeated vomiting can, rarely, cause a tear in the lining of the esophagus, leading to vomiting blood. This needs urgent care.

If your symptoms don't match the typical burning-behind-the-breastbone picture, or they're severe, don't self-treat with antacids. Get medical advice.

## When Frequent Heartburn Becomes a Real Concern

An occasional bout after a big night is normal. Regular heartburn is different. Repeated acid exposure over months and years can inflame the esophagus (esophagitis), cause scarring that narrows it, and in some people lead to changes in the lining called **Barrett's esophagus**, which raises the risk of esophageal cancer. Heavy drinking is also an independent risk factor for some cancers of the esophagus.

That's not meant to frighten you about an occasional bad night. It's a reason not to ignore heartburn that keeps coming back. If you need antacids more than twice a week, or you've been taking acid reducers for longer than the label suggests, see a doctor. They can check what's going on and recommend a treatment plan that's safe for you, which sometimes includes reviewing how much you drink.

## Does Your Gut Health Matter?

Alcohol affects the whole digestive tract, not just the stomach and esophagus. It can change the balance of bacteria in your gut and loosen the barrier of the intestinal lining, which may contribute to bloating and digestive discomfort after drinking. The research here is still developing, but if you notice your digestion is generally worse when you drink, our article on [protecting your gut microbiome from alcohol](/never-hungover/gut-health-alcohol-microbiome-protection) explains what's known.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be clear up front: **there is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) prevents or treats heartburn.** It doesn't neutralize acid, it doesn't tighten the valve, and it shouldn't replace any of the advice above.

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on liver health. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people take it to feel better the morning after drinking, which is a separate goal from avoiding heartburn.

If you want to try DHM for that reason, well-reviewed options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Take it with water, and if you have a sensitive stomach, take it with food. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people use and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol causes heartburn by relaxing the valve between your stomach and esophagus, slowing acid clearance, irritating the lining, and, in the case of beer and wine, boosting acid production.
- The worst combination is large volumes of fizzy, fermented, or acidic drinks plus a heavy late meal and lying down soon after.
- Antacids work fast but briefly. Famotidine helps most when taken before you start, as its label directs. PPIs are for frequent heartburn, not one-off nights.
- Avoid aspirin-based fizzy remedies after drinking.
- Drinking less, choosing still drinks, eating earlier, and staying upright before bed do more than any pill.
- Chest pain that spreads, feels like pressure, or comes with breathlessness or sweating needs emergency care. Heartburn more than twice a week needs a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get heartburn after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, the muscle valve that keeps stomach acid out of your esophagus. It also slows the esophagus's ability to clear acid, irritates the lining, and in the case of beer and wine, stimulates the stomach to make more acid. Fizzy mixers, big late meals, and lying down soon after make it worse.

**What alcohol is least likely to cause heartburn?**

There's no drink that's guaranteed to be heartburn-free, but a small amount of a spirit with still water or a non-citrus, non-fizzy mixer tends to bother people less than beer, champagne, or fizzy cocktails. Research suggests distilled spirits stimulate much less stomach acid than fermented drinks like beer and wine. The amount you drink matters more than the type.

**Can I take Tums or another antacid after drinking?**

For most healthy adults, a standard dose of a calcium-based antacid like Tums after drinking is generally considered fine. It works within minutes but wears off fairly quickly. Stay within the label's daily maximum and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines, since antacids can affect how some drugs are absorbed. Avoid fizzy remedies that contain aspirin, such as Alka-Seltzer Original, after drinking.

**When should I take Pepcid (famotidine) if I'm going to drink?**

The US Pepcid AC label gives directions for preventing heartburn by taking it shortly before eating or drinking things that cause your symptoms, within a window of roughly 15 to 60 minutes. Famotidine isn't known to have a significant interaction with alcohol for most people, but follow the label dose and ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines. If you need it regularly, see a doctor.

**Why is my heartburn worse the morning after drinking?**

Your stomach and esophagus lining can stay irritated for hours after drinking, and sleeping flat with a full stomach allows nighttime reflux. Then a typical hangover breakfast of coffee, orange juice, greasy food, and painkillers like ibuprofen adds more triggers. A bland breakfast, water, and staying upright usually help.

**How long does heartburn from alcohol last?**

For most people, an episode of heartburn after drinking lasts from a few minutes to a few hours and settles once the stomach empties and the lining recovers. If it's still bothering you the next day, or it's lasting longer each time, see a doctor, especially if it happens more than twice a week.

**Can heartburn after drinking be a heart attack?**

It can be hard to tell the difference. Call 911 if chest discomfort feels like pressure or squeezing, spreads to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or lightheadedness. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes are more likely to have heart attack symptoms that feel like indigestion. When in doubt, get checked.

**Does DHM help with heartburn from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats heartburn. It doesn't neutralize acid or affect the valve that keeps acid in your stomach. DHM has been studied for how the body processes alcohol and for liver health, mostly in animals, and some people take it for how they feel the next morning. For heartburn, drinking less, choosing still drinks, eating earlier, and using antacids as directed are the practical steps.
